newsitem.title: GERMANY: German state says it wouldn't pay any EMU fines.
newsitem.headline: German state says it wouldn't pay any EMU fines.

text.p: Saarland, one of Germany's poorest states, would not contribute to pay penalties if the European Union ever fined Bonn for running an excess deficit once the economic and monetary union (EMU) is launched, its finance minister said on Tuesday

Christiane Krajewski, economics and finance minister of the small state bordering France, told German Radio she opposed a plan by several richer states to make the states responsible for any spending overshoot pay the fines for it.

"We are neither ready nor able to pay penalties," she said. As it now stands, all 16 states and the federal government would share the costs of EMU penalties regardless of whether it was Bonn or the states that overspent.

"Germany as a whole took on this commitment to maintain stability according to these agreements on the European level. So (penalties) must be distributed according to fair criteria so that nobody is overburdened," Krajewski said.

Der Spiegel reported on Monday that richer states such as Hesse, Bavaria, Baden-Wuerttemberg and North Rhine-Westphalia wanted the poorer states to pay up if they caused Germany to go over the Maastricht budget deficit target of three percent of gross domestic product or debt target of 60 percent of GDP.
Under a "stability pact" agreed by EU leaders last December in Dublin, any EMU member overshooting the annual deficit target would have to pay the fines.

The richer states already support the poorer ones through a complex financial equalisation scheme. If fines were shared out along those lines, the richer regions would pay once again for states they say are not cutting their budgets enough.
"We want to help, but it isn't right if those who fulfil the Maastricht criteria and reduce their debts are punished because others don't," Hesse state finance minister Karl Starzacher told Spiegel.
Krajewski said a "stability pact" for the states, similar to the strictures Bonn won at the EU level for EMU member states, would overlook economic realities within Germany.
"Of the 16 federal states, at least 12 are structurally weak," she said. They needed "a system that leaves the financially and structurally weak states some air to breathe."

The Social Democrat (SPD) minister noted that Germany's supreme court had ruled in another context that Saarland, an old coal and steel region which France tried to annex after World War Two, was not wholly responsible for its high public deficits and therefore deserved aid from other states.
